analysis.one_liner: Ends taxpayer-subsidized below-cost timber sales in national forests and helps timber towns transition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after subcommittee hearings and one subcommittee session, it stayed in the House Agriculture Committee until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Forest Service from selling national forest timber for less than it costs the government to prepare, administer, and reforest those sales. It also would have removed land that cannot be logged profitably from the timber program, and provided grants, loans, and training to help logging towns build new local economies. The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who currently absorb the losses on below-cost timber sales, plus the forests themselves, since uneconomic logging would be curtailed. Timber workers and their communities would gain access to retraining, grants, and low-interest loans to diversify their local economies.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in October 1997 the bill barred the Forest Service from making any timber sale where expected costs, including road building, sale administration, reforestation, and payments to counties, exceed the revenue returned to the Treasury [S3].
As a transition, it phased down below-cost sales, capping them at 75% of the prior year's level through fiscal 1994, 65% for fiscal 1995, and 50% for fiscal 1996 [S3].
It required the Secretary of Agriculture to identify forest lands where selling timber would lose money and to bar harvesting on those lands for at least 10 years [S3].

It authorized grants to community development corporations in timber-dependent towns for job training, small business development, child care, housing, and other services, with preference for displaced and unemployed timber workers [S3].

It created revolving loan funds offering below-market loans, as low as 1% interest for five years, to families, cooperatives, and businesses in timber-dependent communities, plus family loans of up to $7,500 for housing and self-employment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and mills that relied on cheap national forest timber would pay more or lose access to subsidized sales. Taxpayers would fund the transition assistance appropriations, though the bill's own framing counted stopping sale losses as an offsetting saving.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have reduced the supply of federal timber on a fixed schedule, which timber-dependent towns argued would cost logging and mill jobs faster than new programs could replace them [S3].

The transition assistance was funded by 'such sums as may be necessary' in open-ended appropriations, and the aid authorizations terminated after roughly ten years, creating a funding cliff for communities that did not complete their transition [S3].

Defining a sale's 'costs' requires counting shared overhead, roads, and county payments; critics of cost-recovery rules have argued such accounting gives the agency discretion to shrink or expand the timber program, and the bill left the phase-down percentages tied to prior-year volumes rather than economic need [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: ending below-cost sales saves taxpayers money and stops logging that loses money on every board-foot, but it shrinks timber supply for towns and mills built around it. The bill's answer was a six-year phase-down plus grants and loans for displaced workers, which is a more serious transition package than most such proposals carried. The open-ended appropriations and the ten-year sunset are genuine weaknesses, but the design treats the cost to logging communities directly rather than ignoring it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, got a subcommittee hearing and one subcommittee session in late 1991, and then sat until the Congress ended with no vote in the full committee or on the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Jontz of Indiana and Rep. Robin Ravenel of South Carolina introduced the bill on May 30, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1].
The Agriculture Committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Forests, Family Farms, and Energy, which held hearings on October 30, 1991 [S5].
The subcommittee held a consideration and mark-up session on November 13, 1991, but the action record ends there; the bill never received a vote in the full committee or on the House floor [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and all pending bills die at the end of a Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry kept its access to below-cost national forest timber sales, and taxpayers kept absorbing the losses on those sales. The timber towns the bill aimed to help got no transition aid either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies kept subsidized federal timber

for.name: Rep. Jim Jontz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end below-cost timber sales and provide transition aid to timber towns.

for.name: Rep. Robin Ravenel
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Subcommittee on Forests, Family Farms, and Energy
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill in October 1991 and a consideration and mark-up session on November 13, 1991.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for a House vote after the November 1991 subcommittee session.

against.name: Timber industry
against.role: Buyers of national forest timber sales
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on below-cost timber sales, which supplied mills with federal timber priced below the government's cost.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backers were overwhelmingly Democrats (6 of 7 cosponsors, plus its Democratic sponsor), and it died in a committee controlled by Democrats; no vote was ever taken that would show the split.

industries.note: Mills and loggers bought national forest timber at prices below the government's cost of preparing, administering, road-building, and reforesting the sales, a gap taxpayers covered. The bill phased out those sales and removed uneconomic lands from the timber base, costing the industry cheap supply.

Local logging towns would lose timber sales and jobs, but the bill directed grants, training, and low-interest development loans at displaced workers and their communities. Its interest largely ran alongside that of the workers who lived there.
Below-cost sales meant the Treasury received less than the Forest Service spent to make timber available. Banning them would have ended an ongoing transfer of public money to timber purchasers.
